newsitem.title: USA: Clinton invites lawmakers to discuss foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton invites lawmakers to discuss foreign policy.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and his top foreign policy advisers will meet with key members of Congress on Wednesday night to discuss U.S. policy on international issues ranging from NATO enlargement to engagement with China.

White House spokesman Barry Toiv said Clinton had invited Republican and Democratic leaders of the Senate and House of Representatives to the Blair House meeting, along with the chairmen and ranking members of each congressional committee with national security oversight responsibility.
"It's a chance to exchange views and move help move toward bipartisanship in foreign policy," Toiv said.

He said Clinton had chosen Blair House, an official government guest residence across Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House, as the site of the meeting to allow for an informal give and take over dinner.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Defence Secretary William Cohen and National Security adviser Samuel Berger were among advisers scheduled to take part, Toiv said.

The session between Clinton and the leaders of Congress comes at a time when the administration is struggling to get the Middle East peace process back on track, despite a new cycle of violence between Israel and the Palestinians, and expand the NATO alliance without alienating Russia.

It is also embroiled in controversy over the 1996 Clinton re-election campaign's fund-raising tactics -- a controversy that has raised questions about possible illegal efforts by China to funnel money into the campaign in order to buy U.S. political influence.
Chinese officials have steadfastly denied any interference in the U.S. political process.
Another issue is the administration's drive to win Senate approval of a treaty outlawing chemical weapons before the accord takes effect on April 29.

Toiv said no specific issue or potential for crisis had precipitated the meeting, which was expected to last about three hours. He said it was motivated by Clinton's desire to talk over matters with the lawmakers and promote bipartisan cooperation.
